A document about colour is full of values nobody can read.
`#441100` says nothing; `rgb(10, 100, 200)` says a little less.

`preview-colour` draws the colour next to the code that names it, so a palette, a theme file, or a style guide can be read rather than decoded.

## Installation

```bash
quarto add {{< var extension.reference >}}
```

This will install the extension under the `_extensions` subdirectory.
If you are using version control, you will want to check in this directory.

Or install it from your editor with [Quarto Wizard](https://m.canouil.dev/quarto-wizard):

::: {.btn-group role="group" aria-label="Quarto Wizard installer options"}

[Visual Studio Code](vscode://mcanouil.quarto-wizard/install?repo={{< var extension.wizard-reference >}}){.btn .btn-outline-primary title="Install {{< var extension.reference >}} in Visual Studio Code using the Quarto Wizard extension."}

:::

## Quick start

Enable the filter:

```yaml
filters:
  - preview-colour
```

Then write colours as you would anyway:

```markdown
The brand colour is `#b22222`, with `rgb(10, 100, 200)` for links.
```

The brand colour is `#b22222`, with `rgb(10, 100, 200)` for links.

Inline code is scanned by default; prose is not, until you ask:

```yaml
extensions:
  preview-colour:
    code: true
    text: true
```

This site enables both, so rebeccapurple in ordinary prose is marked too.

::: {.callout-important}
A colour code in inline code has to stand alone.
`` `#441100` `` is recognised; `` `"My colour is #441100"` `` and `` `["#441100", "#114400"]` `` are not.
:::

See the [Reference](reference.qmd) for every format and option, and the [Examples](examples.qmd) for each of them rendered.

## Where it works

HTML, RevealJS, LaTeX, Beamer, Typst, Word, and PowerPoint.

Each gets a glyph appropriate to it, and the [Reference](reference.qmd#format-coverage) records which formats can show transparency and which fall back to the opaque colour.
